entry.title: Caller v State of NSW [2026] NSWCA 212
entry.content:
The appellant, a former NSW police officer, suffered PTSD from cumulative exposure to traumatic incidents during service. The primary judge found the State breached its duty by failing to implement its own record-keeping system to monitor cumulative trauma exposure, but held the breach did not cause the PTSD. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, upholding the no-causation finding and rejecting challenges to other alleged breaches.

Key holding: In a negligence claim, the plaintiff must prove not only breach of duty but also that the breach caused the loss claimed.

In order to succeed on the negligence claim brought by the appellant, it was necessary for him to establish that there was a breach of duty owed to him which caused the loss (in this case, his developing PTSD).

New South Wales Court of Appeal, 13 Oct 2026, [2026] NSWCA 212

entry.title: Costantino v Hillier (No 2) [2026] NSWSC 1260
entry.content:
This is a costs decision following the Court’s earlier determination of limitations issues in a professional negligence claim. The plaintiff failed to obtain an extension of the long-stop limitation period for claims concerning the first four surgeries, while the defendant’s separate question also affected claims concerning the fifth and sixth surgeries. The Court ordered the costs of the plaintiff’s notice of motion and the separate question to be costs in the cause, rather than acceding to the defendant’s proposed 75% costs order.

Key holding: Where parties achieve mixed success on overlapping interlocutory limitation applications, the Court may exercise its costs discretion by ordering costs in the cause rather than apportioning costs issue-by-issue.

In my view, the parties have each achieved some success and some failure in their competing applications which were heard before me on 18 and 19 August 2026. While there is some significant overlap between them, I nevertheless consider the most appropriate way to approach the costs of those applications is to order that they be costs in the cause.

Supreme Court of New South Wales, 12 Oct 2026, [2026] NSWSC 1260

entry.title: Palmer v State of Queensland [2026] QSC 30
entry.content:
The plaintiff sued the State of Queensland for psychiatric injury allegedly caused by a rape on Palm Island in about 1959 or 1960, when she was a child. The State applied for summary judgment or strike-out, denying any duty of care and alleging no causal link. The Supreme Court entered judgment for the State and ordered the plaintiff to pay costs.

Key holding: If the material does not suggest a party could plead a legally recognised cause of action, leave to replead should be refused and judgment for the defendant may follow.

Where there is nothing in the material before the court to suggest that a party could plead a cause of action known to law, leave to replead would be refused. Indeed, a logical consequence may be to give judgment for the defendant.

Supreme Court of Queensland, 12 Oct 2026, [2026] QSC 30

entry.title: SC (name suppressed) v Integroe Partners Pty Ltd t/as Integroe Partners [2026] NSWDC 367
entry.content:
The Plaintiff, the mother of a child (PS) treated at a Sydney Catholic Schools school, sued Integroe Partners Pty Ltd in negligence over investigations it conducted for SCS into the school’s use of a sensory room and lockdown procedures. She alleged the Defendant owed her a duty of care as a non-client, breached it, and caused her psychiatric injury. The District Court dismissed the proceedings and ordered costs against the Plaintiff.

Key holding: A law firm retained by an institutional client does not owe a third-party complainant a duty of care merely because it investigates that complainant’s concerns; such a relationship falls outside established duty categories and is assessed as a novel duty by salient features.

In my opinion, the relationship between the Plaintiff and the Defendant does not fall within any established categories of relationship that give rise to a duty of care. The Plaintiff was a third party to the professional/client relationship between the Defendant and SCS.

entry.title: Zvicer v Hunter New England Local Health District [2026] NSWSC 1241
entry.content:
Ms Zvicer sued Hunter New England Local Health District alleging that hospital doctors negligently failed to perform a fasciotomy on her left lower leg on 11 November 2020, causing a below-knee amputation. Her children separately claimed psychiatric injury. The Supreme Court dismissed all claims, rejecting liability.

Key holding: A defendant is not liable in negligence for harm that is the materialisation of an inherent risk, being a risk that could not be avoided by reasonable care and skill.

A person is not liable in negligence for harm suffered by another person as a result of the materialisation of an inherent risk.

entry.title: Soar Development Group Pty Ltd v Fung [2026] FCA 1491
entry.content:
Soar sought leave to amend its originating application and statement of claim in a Federal Court commercial proceeding, including professional negligence and knowing assistance claims against EFG and Mr Huang. The first to fourth respondents did not oppose, but EFG and Mr Huang opposed certain amendments on delay and prejudice grounds, saying they materially enlarged the case and loss shortly before a combined hearing.

Key holding: The court may grant leave to amend closed pleadings under rr 8.21 and 16.53 in the exercise of a broad discretion informed by the overarching purpose, and may impose conditions including costs and timetable relief to address delay and prejudice.

An order granting leave may be made subject to conditions: r 1.33. The discretion to grant leave is broad, but must be exercised in a manner consistent with the overarching purpose stated in s 37M of the Federal Court of Australia Act 1976 (Cth) (FCA Act), namely to facilitate the just resolution of disputes according to law and as quickly, inexpensively and efficiently as possible.

entry.title: Mellick v Samarasekera and Ors [2026] NSWSC 1239
entry.content:
This was an application in the Supreme Court of New South Wales for expedition of medical negligence proceedings brought by George Mellick, by his tutor, against two general practitioners and South Western Sydney Local Health District. The plaintiff is 21 years old, has a limited life expectancy and remains at risk of sudden death. The Court granted expedition, fixed an expedited hearing and made case-management directions.

Key holding: In fixing an expedited hearing date that will impose intense preparation burdens, the plaintiff’s health is the primary consideration where the parties agree an early date is required.

I appreciate fixing the matter for hearing on 15 March 2027 will visit an intense period of preparation upon the parties and that some counsel will have to be swapped out due to prior professional commitments, however in all the circumstances the health of the plaintiff needs to be the primary consideration here and the parties have agreed that an early date needs to be accommodated.

entry.title: Youssef & Ors v Dr Sekharipuram Ramamvrthi Govind Krishna [2026] NSWSC 1253
entry.content:
Coleman J approved settlements of claims brought by two minor plaintiffs, Isaiah (16) and Savannah (14), against Dr Krishna for pure mental harm/nervous shock allegedly arising from witnessing their mother’s complications after bariatric surgery. The proceedings were conducted by their father as tutor. Because the plaintiffs are under legal incapacity, the settlements required court approval under s 76(4) of the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW).

Key holding: On an application to approve a settlement for a person under legal incapacity, the court’s protective function requires it to determine whether the settlement is beneficial to that person’s interests.

The Court's function on such an application is essentially protective. The Court ought to review the terms of settlement or compromise to protect the interests of the persons under the legal incapacity

entry.title: Frazer v State of Queensland [2026] QSC 82 (22 April 2026)
entry.content:
Ms Frazer, an experienced teacher, sued the State of Queensland after suffering PTSD following an incident where an aggrieved parent attended the school looking to confront her. The State admitted it owed a non-delegable duty of care to Ms Frazer, but disputed breach. The court found no breach and entered judgment for the defendant.

Key holding: A policy authorising physical force to remove an abusive or threatening person does not require force in every circumstance; reasonableness depends on the unfolding situation.

It seems to me that the authorisation in Chief Executive Guideline No 1 of 2012 to take all reasonable steps including physical force to eject an abusive, threatening or disorderly person does not, could not and should not demand in all circumstances that physical force be used to eject an abusive, threatening or disorderly person.

entry.title: Shorland Fisheries Pty Ltd & Ors v State of Victoria [2026] VSC 29 (16 February 2026)
entry.content:
Fifteen commercial abalone fishers sued the State of Victoria in negligence after two Crown leases were granted over their fishing grounds without the mandatory public notice required by s 137 of the Land Act 1958 (Vic). The leases gave the lessee (MAPA Pearls) indefeasible title and exclusive possession, locking the fishers out of the lease areas for up to 31 years. Watson J found the State liable, holding that all three public servants owed and breached a duty of care, causation was established, and damages were awarded.

entry.title: AA v The Trustees of the Roman Catholic Church for the Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle [2026] HCA 2 (11 February 2026)
entry.content:
The High Court allowed an appeal by a victim of historic child sexual abuse by a Catholic priest in 1969, holding that the Diocese of Maitland-Newcastle owed the appellant (then a 13-year-old child) a non-delegable duty of care. The Court re-opened and overturned the majority position in New South Wales v Lepore (2003) 212 CLR 511 that a non-delegable duty cannot extend to harm caused by intentional criminal acts, restoring judgment in favour of the appellant with damages adjusted under the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW).

entry.title: Body Corporate for Westmark Milton CTS v Devine Constructions Pty Ltd [2026] QSC 9 (27 January 2026)
entry.content:
The Supreme Court of Queensland considered whether a body corporate can sue a builder in its own name for defective construction work on common property, relying on s 36(3) of the Body Corporate and Community Management Act 1997 (Qld) (BCCMA). The builder argued "subrogated" in s 36(3) carried its technical equitable meaning, requiring the body corporate to sue in the original owner's name. Ryan J rejected that argument, declaring the body corporate entitled to proceed in its own name.
